1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text:
Basic information: Female, 45 years old, from Nanjing, Jiangsu. Chief complaint: "fever for 5 days." She was admitted to the inpatient Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, Nanjing Jiangning Hospital, on Day 0.

Five days before admission, the patient developed fever without an obvious precipitating factor, with Tmax 39.5℃, accompanied by chills and headache, without obvious discomfort such as cough, sputum production, chest tightness, or hemoptysis. On Day -2, she presented to our hospital's fever clinic. Complete blood count showed: PLT 86×10^9/L, WBC 5.16×10^9/L, N 74.00%, L 18.20%↓, CRP 41.29mg/l↑. Chest CT suggested inflammation in the left lower lobe. She was admitted to our hospital for further treatment. Since the onset of illness, her mental status and sleep have been fair, appetite poor, bowel and bladder function normal, and weight without obvious change.

The patient was previously in good health. She denied a history of chronic diseases such as "hypertension" and "diabetes mellitus." She denied a history of infectious diseases such as "hepatitis" and "TB," as well as exposure history. She denied a history of major trauma and blood transfusion, and denied food and drug allergies. Immunizations were up to date per routine. She was born and has lived in her native place, and denied contact with contaminated water or epidemic areas. She denied tobacco, alcohol, and drug/toxin exposure history. She denied any significant family history.

After admission, we first performed a physical examination: T 36.6℃, P 85/min, R 20/min, BP 105/60mmHg. The patient was alert, with fair general condition. No rash was present on the skin. No enlarged lymph nodes were palpable throughout the body. The thorax showed no deformity. Bilateral chest expansion was symmetric. Tactile fremitus was not increased. Percussion of both lungs was resonant. On auscultation, breath sounds were clear in both lungs; a small amount of moist rales was heard in the left lower lung. No Velcro rales were heard, and no pleural friction rub was heard.

There was no precordial bulge. The apical impulse was located at the fifth intercostal space, 0.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line. No thrill was palpable. Cardiac borders were not enlarged. Heart rate was 85/min, rhythm regular, with no obvious increase or decrease in heart sounds, and no pathologic murmur was heard in any valve auscultation area. The abdomen was flat and soft, with no hepatosplenomegaly, no abdominal tenderness, and no abdominal muscle guarding. No edema was present in either lower extremity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Community-acquired pneumonia (left lower lobe pneumonia, predominantly bacterial)
supporting_evidence: Chief complaint: fever for 5 days, Tmax 39.5℃, accompanied by chills and headache
CRP 41.29 mg/L ↑, indicating the presence of an inflammatory response
Chest CT showed inflammation in the left lower lobe of the lung
On the first-phase images, a patchy subpleural area of consolidation/exudative opacity is visible in the left lower lung.
Physical examination: a few moist crackles were heard in the left lower lung.
opposing_evidence: No obvious respiratory symptoms such as cough, sputum production, chest tightness, or hemoptysis.
WBC 5.16×10^9/L, no significant leukocytosis observed
PLT 86×10^9/L, not a typical blood count finding of simple common bacterial pneumonia

differential_diagnoses.name: Viral pneumonia (including possible SARS-CoV-2 infection)
supporting_evidence: Fever as the main manifestation, Tmax 39.5℃, accompanied by headache
WBC 5.16×10^9/L, L 18.20%↓, may be seen in viral infection
Chest CT showed inflammation in the left lower lobe; first-stage images showed patchy exudative opacities in the left lower lung.
Respiratory symptoms are relatively not prominent; only pulmonary lesions are present on imaging.
opposing_evidence: On the first-stage images, the lesion is more focal left lower lobe consolidation, rather than a typical bilateral multifocal diffuse distribution.
A few moist rales in the left lower lung and elevated CRP may also further support bacterial pneumonia
The first-stage information did not provide a definite epidemiologic exposure history.

differential_diagnoses.name: Atypical pathogen pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella, etc.)
supporting_evidence: Marked fever accompanied by headache, but without obvious cough or sputum production, consistent with some clinical features of atypical pneumonia
WBC 5.16×10^9/L was not significantly elevated, whereas CRP 41.29mg/l ↑
Chest CT showed inflammation in the left lower lobe; first-stage images showed focal exudative/consolidative opacity in the left lower lung.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not provide clues such as myalgia, diarrhea, and hyponatremia that would more strongly support specific atypical pathogens.
Although a PLT of 86×10^9/L can be seen in infection, it is not specific evidence for atypical pneumonia.
The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis (atypical pulmonary tuberculosis with onset as a lesion in the left lower lobe)
supporting_evidence: Fever for 5 days, which may be a manifestation of an infectious disease
Chest CT suggests inflammatory changes in the left lower lobe; first-phase images show a focal lesion in the left lower lung, which should be differentiated from an infectious granulomatous lesion.
Thrombocytopenia can be seen in the setting of some infectious diseases
opposing_evidence: Relatively acute onset, with a disease course of only 5 days, more suggestive of acute infection
Denies a history of TB or other infectious diseases and any exposure history
No common indicators suggestive of TB, such as cough, hemoptysis, or marked weight change
The images from the first stage show focal consolidation in the left lower lobe, which is not a typical upper lobe/posterior segment-predominant pattern.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction
supporting_evidence: Fever may occur as part of the inflammatory response after pulmonary infarction.
Images from the first stage show a focal subpleural consolidation in the left lower lung, morphologically distinguishable from a pulmonary infarction lesion.
No obvious cough or sputum production; when pulmonary symptoms do not completely correlate with imaging lesions, noninfectious lesions should be considered.
opposing_evidence: No common manifestations of pulmonary embolism such as chest pain, dyspnea, or hemoptysis
Vital signs were relatively stable, P 85 beats/min, R 20 breaths/min, BP 105/60 mmHg
A few moist rales in the left lower lung on physical examination, elevated CRP, and a CT report of "left lower lobe inflammation" more strongly support infection.
The phase 1 information did not provide a history of venous thromboembolism risk factors or prolonged bed rest.

differential_diagnoses.name: Thrombocytopenia associated with hematologic disease or systemic infection with secondary pulmonary infection
supporting_evidence: PLT 86×10^9/L, definite thrombocytopenia is present
Fever for 5 days, with CRP 41.29mg/l↑, suggesting the presence of an infectious/inflammatory process
Chest CT suggested inflammatory changes in the left lower lobe; phase 1 images showed consolidation in the left lower lung, possibly a secondary pulmonary infectious focus.
opposing_evidence: Previously healthy; physical examination showed no hepatosplenomegaly, no generalized rash, and no palpable lymphadenopathy, with no obvious supportive evidence of a hematologic disorder
WBC 5.16×10^9/L, no obvious abnormalities in the three cell lineages
The stage 1 information did not provide evidence of a bleeding tendency, manifestations of anemia, or other systemic involvement.

recommended_exams.exam: Complete blood count and inflammatory markers
Nine respiratory pathogen panel, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia antibodies

stage2_input.text:
Laboratory tests:
1. Routine parameters:
[Arterial blood gas analysis] pH 7.49, PCO2 36 mmHg, PO2 82 mmHg (not receiving oxygen).
[Complete blood count and inflammatory markers] PLT 113×10^9/L, WBC 3.54×10^9/L, N 66.60%, L 24.50%, CRP 57.62 mg/L.
[Urinalysis, stool routine + OB] normal.
[Biochemical parameters] albumin 37.1 g/L, potassium 2.88 mmol/L, no significant abnormalities in liver or kidney function.
[Coagulation function, procalcitonin] normal.
2. Pathogen and tumor-related markers
[Pre-transfusion eight-item panel] normal.
[Fungi] GM test (-).
[Viruses] nine-item respiratory pathogen panel, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia antibodies (-).
[Tuberculosis] TB infection T-cell test (-).
3. Pulmonary HRCT
(Day -2, Figure 1) Consolidation in the left lower lung, considered inflammation; follow-up reexamination recommended after treatment.
4. Bronchoscopy + bronchoalveolar lavage:
(Day -364) No abnormalities were seen on bronchoscopy. After lavage of the basal segment of the left lower lung, sputum was collected for testing. Submitted for differential cell count; Gram stain, bacterial culture, fungal culture, and BALF mNGS.
5. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid results:
[Pathogen testing] No bacteria seen, no fungi detected; acid-fast stain: no acid-fast bacilli seen; [Differential cell count] total cell count 118×10^6/L, macrophages 70.0%, lymphocytes 15.00%, neutrophils 13.00%, eosinophils 2.00%.
Ancillary examinations: ① Chest CT: ground-glass opacity in the left lower lung; ② Arterial blood gas analysis: basically normal; ③ Complete blood count and inflammatory markers: thrombocytopenia, elevated inflammatory markers; ④ BAIF cytologic differential: total cell count 118×10^6/L, macrophages 70.0%, lymphocytes 15.00%, neutrophils 13.00%, eosinophils 2.00%.

images.near_text: Infiltrative pulmonary tuberculosis, peripheral lung cancer, or pneumonia?

differential_diagnoses.name: Infiltrative pulmonary tuberculosis
evidence: If the patient has cough and sputum production for more than 2 or 3 weeks, and symptomatic treatment and anti-infective therapy are ineffective, there is a high likelihood that the appearance of patchy pulmonary opacities is caused by pulmonary TB.

differential_diagnoses.name: Peripheral lung cancer
evidence: A small proportion of patients may be asymptomatic and are often identified by patchy pulmonary opacities on imaging studies. Most patients may present with cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, or wheezing.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pneumonia (bacterial, atypical pathogen, viral, fungal, other pathogens, due to physical and chemical factors)
evidence: A middle-aged woman with acute onset was admitted for fever for 5 days. After admission, inflammatory markers were mildly elevated, platelet count was decreased, and chest HRCT showed inflammatory changes in the left lower lung with visible consolidation. This was also accompanied by electrolyte disturbance; therefore, an infectious disease was considered more likely.

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had an acute onset, with fever for 5 days, with a maximum temperature of 39.5℃, accompanied by chills and headache. Chest CT/HRCT showed a focal inflammatory lesion in the left lower lung, but respiratory symptoms such as cough and sputum production were not prominent, and the CBC showed that the white blood cell count was not elevated or was even low, with thrombocytopenia. Routine respiratory pathogen antibody testing, the GM test, and TB infection T-cell testing did not provide a clear etiology, and there was insufficient evidence in the direction of routine bacteriology. On further questioning, it was then found that approximately half a month before onset there was a definite history of contact with parrots, especially sick or dead birds, suggesting that atypical pathogens, especially Chlamydia psittaci infection, should be strongly considered. Bronchoscopy can directly assess whether there are visible airway lesions, bleeding, masses, or purulent secretions, and can precisely obtain a bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimen from the segment corresponding to the left lower lung lesion, thereby improving the pathogen detection rate. The core clinical purpose of this examination is, when routine noninvasive testing is inconclusive, to further confirm an infectious etiology, exclude peripheral lung cancer, TB, and other noninfectious lesions, and create the conditions for subsequent lavage fluid culture, staining, and mNGS testing, thereby guiding the selection of the anti-infective regimen. The patient's arterial blood gas was basically normal, and vital signs were overall stable, also indicating relative feasibility for performing this invasive examination.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Final BALF mNGS showed: Haemophilus parainfluenzae (sequence count 314), Haemophilus influenzae (sequence count 209), Staphylococcus aureus (sequence count 20), Streptococcus pneumoniae (sequence count 19), Chlamydia psittaci (sequence count 13).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This patient presented mainly with high fever, chills, and headache. Chest imaging showed only a focal area of consolidation/ground-glass inflammatory opacity in the left lower lung, with relatively mild respiratory symptoms. The blood count showed a WBC count that was not elevated or even decreased, decreased PLT, normal procalcitonin, negative routine respiratory pathogen antibodies, fungal GM, and TB-related tests, and no abnormalities were seen on bronchoscopy. Routine bacterial and fungal cultures and acid-fast staining of BALF failed to identify the pathogen. Therefore, there was a situation of "clinically highly suspected infection but negative by traditional etiologic testing." Combined with the definite history obtained during hospitalization of contact with parrots and dead birds, the key clinical question was whether there was infection with atypical, intracellular, or difficult-to-culture pathogens such as Chlamydia psittaci. BALF mNGS has advantages for detecting pathogens that are not easily identified by routine culture and can more comprehensively identify bacteria, atypical pathogens, and others in a single test. This would not only help confirm Chlamydia psittaci infection, but also identify whether other bacterial pathogens were present, thereby explaining the patient's persistent high fever and imaging findings of pneumonia. The results of this test directly affect the direction of the differential diagnosis, the spectrum of antimicrobial coverage, and whether targeted treatment such as doxycycline should be selected, while avoiding prolonged empiric and blind medication use.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text:
During the patient's hospitalization, we continuously and meticulously explored details of the patient's daily life, analyzed many behaviors before and after disease onset together with the patient, and guided the patient to repeatedly recall aspects that had not been noticed in daily life. During one conversation, the patient casually mentioned that for a period of time he had been very fond of visiting flower-and-bird markets. After seeing how cute the parrots raised by others were, he suddenly became interested in keeping birds, so he bought 3 small parrots, but because he was not careful enough, 2 parrots soon became ill and died... This occurred approximately half a month before his disease onset. After learning this information, we immediately became highly alert. The patient had a definite history of parrot exposure, especially exposure to sick and dead birds. Based on the epidemiologic characteristics of this region, atypical pathogens were highly suspected, especially Chlamydia psittaci.
The team quickly completed bronchoscopy, and mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid ultimately showed: Haemophilus parainfluenzae (sequence count 314), Haemophilus influenzae (sequence count 209), Staphylococcus aureus (sequence count 20), Streptococcus pneumoniae (sequence count 19), Chlamydia psittaci (sequence count 13).
